etymology: Hebrew qavah (to wait, hope, expect) + LORD; recurring Psalmic and prophetic imperative.
biblical_def: The disciplined posture of expectant trust; not passive idleness but active hope-laden patience. Qavah shares its root with tikvah (hope) — waiting and hoping are one verb in Hebrew. Isaiah 40:31's classic: "they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength."
webster_summary: Disciplined expectant trust; same root as hope.
webster_full: The disciplined posture of expectant trust commanded throughout the Psalms and prophets. Hebrew qavah shares its root with tikvah (hope) — in Hebrew, waiting and hoping are the same verb. Not passive idleness but active hope-laden patience. The classic promise: those who wait on the LORD renew their strength.
scriptures: Isaiah 40:31
But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.
Psalm 27:14
Wait on the LORD: be of good courage, and he shall strengthen thine heart: wait, I say, on the LORD.
Psalm 130:5-6
I wait for the LORD, my soul doth wait, and in his word do I hope.
corruption_summary: Modern impatience-culture has lost the waiting category; productivity culture treats all waiting as wasted time.
corruption_paragraphs: The age has near-zero tolerance for waiting. Scripture treats waiting as the school of hope. The same Hebrew word means both. To wait is to hope; to hope is to wait. The two cannot be separated.
Recover the verb: waiting on the LORD is active soul-work. The eagle rises only after the wind comes; the saint rises only after waiting renews.
usage: Wait on the LORD; be of good courage.
Waiting and hoping are one Hebrew verb.
Eagles wait for the wind.

etymology: Hebrew baqash panim — to seek the face / presence; recurring Psalmic and prophetic command.
biblical_def: The pursuit of God's manifest presence rather than merely His benefits. To seek His face (panim) is to seek personal nearness with the Person, not transactional access to power or gifts. The Aaronic blessing prays His face shine upon us; the saint reciprocates by seeking the face that shines.
webster_summary: Pursuit of God's personal nearness, not just His benefits.
webster_full: The Hebrew idiom for seeking God's manifest personal presence. Panim (face) signifies presence, person, and relational intimacy. To seek His face is to want Him — not just His gifts, His help, or His blessing — but Him. The Aaronic blessing of Numbers 6:25 prays "the LORD make his face shine upon thee"; the saint's response is to seek that face.
scriptures: Psalm 27:8
When thou saidst, Seek ye my face; my heart said unto thee, Thy face, LORD, will I seek.
1 Chronicles 16:11
Seek the LORD and his strength, seek his face continually.
2 Chronicles 7:14
If my people, which are called by my name, shall humble themselves, and pray, and seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then will I hear from heaven.
corruption_summary: Reduced to seeking benefits or answers; the Person-of-God is the actual object Scripture commands seeking.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern Christian seeking often pursues outcomes (healing, guidance, breakthrough). Scripture's seek-his-face is more demanding and more restful: pursue the Person, and the outcomes follow Him. The face is the destination, not the means.
Recover the priority: His face first; His hand second.
usage: Thy face, LORD, will I seek.
Seek His face continually.
Pursue the Person; outcomes follow Him.

etymology: Hebrew anag / chaphets with YHWH; cherished Psalmic command.
biblical_def: The disposition of soul-satisfaction in YHWH Himself, often with the promise that He will give the desires of such a heart (Ps 37:4). The order matters: delight first, then desires fulfilled — because the delighting heart's desires conform to His.
webster_summary: Soul-satisfaction in YHWH Himself.
webster_full: The disposition of soul-satisfaction taking pleasure in YHWH Himself, not merely in His gifts. Psalm 37:4's promise rides on the order: "Delight thyself also in the LORD; and he shall give thee the desires of thine heart" — the delighting heart's desires increasingly conform to His, so what He gives is what the heart now wants.
scriptures: Psalm 37:4
Delight thyself also in the LORD; and he shall give thee the desires of thine heart.
Psalm 1:2
But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night.
Isaiah 58:13-14
If thou turn away thy foot from the sabbath... and call the sabbath a delight... then shalt thou delight thyself in the LORD.
corruption_summary: Psalm 37:4 misread as a wish-fulfillment formula; the verse depends on the order.
corruption_paragraphs: Pop-Christianity reads Psalm 37:4 as: tell God what you want; delight a little; receive. The Hebrew order is sterner: delight in HIM, and the desires that emerge are the ones He gives you. The promise is that you will want what He gives, not that He will give what you currently want.
Recover the order: delight is the prior gift; aligned desires are the result.
usage: Delight thyself in the LORD — then desires.
His law is the delighter's meditation.
Sabbath as delight is delight in the LORD.

etymology: Hebrew nasa einayim — to lift up eyes; the deliberate redirection of gaze.
biblical_def: The deliberate act of redirecting one's gaze — from the immediate to the eternal, from the trouble to the help, from the self to the LORD. Psalm 121's pilgrim opener: "I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help." The verb is a discipline.
webster_summary: Deliberate redirection of gaze toward the LORD.
webster_full: The Hebrew idiom for deliberately redirecting the gaze, often used of looking from earthly trouble to heavenly help. Psalm 121 opens with the pilgrim's lifting of eyes; Genesis 13's Abram lifting his eyes to receive the land-promise; Isaiah 40's "Lift up your eyes on high, and behold who hath created these things." The verb is a discipline of attention.
scriptures: Psalm 121:1-2
I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help. My help cometh from the LORD, which made heaven and earth.
Isaiah 40:26
Lift up your eyes on high, and behold who hath created these things, that bringeth out their host by number: he calleth them all by names.
Genesis 13:14
And the LORD said unto Abram... Lift up now thine eyes, and look from the place where thou art northward, and southward, and eastward, and westward.
corruption_summary: Phone-and-screen culture has trained downward gaze; the discipline of lifting eyes upward is increasingly counter-cultural.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern attention is trained downward — phones in laps, screens at eye-level. Scripture's lift-up-eyes is the opposite discipline: looking up, looking out, looking long. The pilgrim looks to the hills; the saint looks to the heavens.
Recover the upward gaze: literal and figurative. Look up at the stars tonight. Look up at the heavens. Lift up your eyes — the help comes from there.
usage: I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills.
Lift up your eyes on high — behold the Creator.
Discipline of upward attention.

etymology: Hebrew natah ozen — to bend / stretch the ear; the posture of attentive listening.
biblical_def: The deliberate act of bending the ear toward the speaker, the active discipline of attentive listening. Used both of God inclining His ear to hear the saint's prayer, and of the saint inclining the ear to hear God's word. The verb names listening as bodily posture.
webster_summary: The bending of the ear toward the speaker; deliberate attention.
webster_full: The Hebrew idiom for deliberately leaning the ear toward the speaker. Used both ways: God inclines His ear to the saint's prayer (Ps 17:6; 31:2), and the saint inclines the ear to God's word (Prov 4:20; 5:1). The image is bodily — you literally lean into the conversation. Listening is not passive reception but active posture.
scriptures: Psalm 17:6
I have called upon thee, for thou wilt hear me, O God: incline thine ear unto me, and hear my speech.
Proverbs 4:20
My son, attend to my words; incline thine ear unto my sayings.
Isaiah 55:3
Incline your ear, and come unto me: hear, and your soul shall live.
corruption_summary: Distracted-listening culture (half-hearing, multi-tasking) is the opposite; biblical listening is bodily-engaged.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern listening is half-listening — ears half-engaged while attention runs elsewhere. Scripture's inclining is bodily: the listener bends toward the speaker. God leans toward His people in prayer; we are to lean toward Him in His word.
Recover the bodily posture: when reading Scripture, lean in. When praying, picture God leaning in to hear. The verb works both directions.
usage: Incline thine ear, O LORD — the prayer.
Incline thine ear, my son — the wisdom call.
Listening is bodily, not just mental.

etymology: Hebrew shalak yehab (Ps 55:22); Greek epirrhiptō merimna (1 Pet 5:7).
biblical_def: The deliberate transfer of weight from one's own shoulders to YHWH's. Psalm 55:22's command: "Cast thy burden upon the LORD, and he shall sustain thee." Picked up by Peter: "casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you" (1 Pet 5:7). Active verb — you must cast.
webster_summary: Active transfer of weight from self to YHWH.
webster_full: The deliberate, active transfer of weight from one's own shoulders to the LORD's. Psalm 55:22's shalak yehab — "throw your burden" — is sharper than "hand it over"; it is a hurling. Peter picks up the same verb in Greek epirrhiptō (literally "to throw upon"): "casting all your care upon him." Worry retains the burden; faith hurls it.
scriptures: Psalm 55:22
Cast thy burden upon the LORD, and he shall sustain thee: he shall never suffer the righteous to be moved.
1 Peter 5:7
Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you.
Matthew 11:28-30
Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls.
corruption_summary: Modern "give it to God" sometimes means just praying about it without actually releasing it; the biblical verb is more decisive.
corruption_paragraphs: "Give it to God" can become a phrase that doesn't actually transfer weight. Hebrew shalak and Greek epirrhiptō are sharper — throw it, hurl it, deliberately set it down on Him. The act is decisive.
Recover the verb: the burden is not light because we have grown strong; the burden is light because we have hurled it onto the One who sustains.
usage: Cast thy burden upon the LORD.
Cast it; do not just talk about it.
Faith hurls; worry retains.

etymology: Hebrew tsel kenaphayim; recurring Psalmic image of refuge under the wings of YHWH.
biblical_def: The recurring Psalmic image of refuge under the protective wings of YHWH — chicks gathered under the hen, the saint hidden under the Almighty. Boaz uses it of Ruth ("under whose wings thou art come to trust," Ruth 2:12); Christ uses it lamenting Jerusalem ("as a hen gathereth her chickens," Matt 23:37).
webster_summary: Refuge under YHWH's protective wings; recurring Psalmic image.
webster_full: The recurring Psalmic image of refuge taken under the protective wings of YHWH — the chick under the hen, the saint hidden under the Almighty. Used of Ruth ("under whose wings thou art come to trust"), throughout the Psalms ("in the shadow of thy wings will I make my refuge," Ps 57:1), and by Christ Himself lamenting Jerusalem ("as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings"). The cherubim's wings over the mercy seat may underlie the imagery.
scriptures: Psalm 91:4
He shall cover thee with his feathers, and under his wings shalt thou trust: his truth shall be thy shield and buckler.
Ruth 2:12
The LORD recompense thy work, and a full reward be given thee of the LORD God of Israel, under whose wings thou art come to trust.
Matthew 23:37
O Jerusalem, Jerusalem... how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!
corruption_summary: Sentimentalized to greeting-card warmth; the actual image (chick hiding under mother in storm) is muscular protection.
corruption_paragraphs: Pop usage of "under His wings" sounds soft. The actual image is sharp: predator approaches, chicks dive under hen's spread wings, hen sustains the blow if any. The hen dies before the chicks do. The picture is muscular protection, not cozy comfort.
Recover the protection: the wings absorb the blow. Christ on the cross is the Hen who covered the chicks at her own cost.
usage: Under His wings shalt thou trust.
Boaz to Ruth: under YHWH's wings.
The Hen covers chicks at her own cost.

etymology: Hebrew seter (covering, hiding place); central image of Psalm 91.
biblical_def: The hidden, intimate refuge of YHWH's presence. Psalm 91:1's opener: "He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty." The saint's life is sustained by a private, hidden communion with God that observers do not see.
webster_summary: The hidden refuge of YHWH's intimate presence.
webster_full: The hidden, intimate refuge of YHWH's presence. Psalm 91:1 opens with the conditional: he that dwelleth in the secret place. The dwelling is the qualifier. The Hebrew seter means a covering, hiding place, secrecy. Christ commands prayer in the secret place (Matt 6:6), where the Father sees in secret. The hidden life with God sustains the visible life with men.
scriptures: Psalm 91:1
He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty.
Matthew 6:6
But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly.
Psalm 27:5
For in the time of trouble he shall hide me in his pavilion: in the secret of his tabernacle shall he hide me.
corruption_summary: Public-platform Christianity has lost the secret-place; what cannot be photographed often is not cultivated.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern Christianity is heavily public — platforms, cameras, social-share. Scripture's secret place is the opposite: hidden, intimate, unphotographed. The Father sees in secret; what He sees there builds the visible life that no platform can sustain.
Recover the hidden room: closet, knees, dawn, alone. Where no one sees but Him, the actual life with God grows.
usage: He that dwelleth in the secret place — the conditional.
Pray to thy Father which is in secret.
The hidden life sustains the visible life.

etymology: Hebrew seter; David's repeated image for YHWH as personal refuge.
biblical_def: YHWH Himself as the saint's hiding place from trouble. Psalm 32:7's: "Thou art my hiding place; thou shalt preserve me from trouble." Distinct from earthly hiding places (which fail) — YHWH-as-hiding-place is sufficient and sure.
webster_summary: YHWH as personal hiding place from trouble.
webster_full: Davidic image of YHWH Himself as the saint's hiding place. Psalm 32:7 names it directly: "Thou art my hiding place." Psalm 119:114: "Thou art my hiding place and my shield." The image runs through Scripture and into Christian devotional history (Corrie ten Boom's The Hiding Place). Earthly hiding places fail; YHWH does not.
scriptures: Psalm 32:7
Thou art my hiding place; thou shalt preserve me from trouble; thou shalt compass me about with songs of deliverance.
Psalm 119:114
Thou art my hiding place and my shield: I hope in thy word.
Isaiah 32:2
And a man shall be as an hiding place from the wind, and a covert from the tempest; as rivers of water in a dry place, as the shadow of a great rock in a weary land.
corruption_summary: Modern self-reliance treats hiding as weakness; biblical hiding in YHWH is the wise refuge.
corruption_paragraphs: Self-reliance culture treats "hiding" as cowardice. Scripture treats hiding in the LORD as wisdom. There is shame-hiding (Adam from God) and refuge-hiding (David in God). The first kind is sin's reflex; the second is faith's discipline.
Recover the refuge: when trouble comes, hide in the LORD. He compasses His own about with songs of deliverance.
usage: Thou art my hiding place; preserve me.
Refuge-hiding, not shame-hiding.
Songs of deliverance compass the hidden.

etymology: Hebrew neot deshe (Ps 23:2) — tender pastures of grass.
biblical_def: Psalm 23:2's image of YHWH as Shepherd making the saint lie down in tender, well-watered pasture. Not just grazing-ground but rest-ground — the sheep lies down only when full and at peace. The Shepherd's provision is total enough that lying down becomes possible.
webster_summary: Psalm 23:2 image of total provision producing rest.
webster_full: Psalm 23:2's image of the Shepherd making His sheep lie down in tender pastures. Sheep do not lie down when hungry, thirsty, or anxious; they only lie down when full and at peace. The Shepherd's provision is therefore total — food, water, safety — producing the rest that lying-down represents. The Hebrew neot deshe is literally "meadows of tender grass."
scriptures: Psalm 23:2
He maketh me to lie down in green pastures: he leadeth me beside the still waters.
Ezekiel 34:14
I will feed them in a good pasture, and upon the high mountains of Israel shall their fold be.
John 10:9
I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved, and shall go in and out, and find pasture.
corruption_summary: Sentimentalized as gentle rest-image; misses that lying-down requires total provision first.
corruption_paragraphs: Greeting-card readings of Psalm 23:2 emphasize the green and the pasture. The verb is the gospel: "He maketh me to lie down." Sheep that aren't full and safe don't lie down. The Shepherd provides so completely that rest becomes possible.
Recover the verb: the gift is not just the pasture but the lying-down. Provision produces rest; rest is a gift.
usage: He maketh me to lie down — the gift.
Sheep lie down only when full and safe.
Total provision produces rest.

etymology: Hebrew mei menuchot (Ps 23:2) — literally "waters of rest."
biblical_def: Psalm 23:2's image of YHWH as Shepherd leading the saint beside calm, drinkable water. Sheep cannot drink from rushing or muddy water; the Shepherd seeks the still places where the flock can be refreshed. The Hebrew mei menuchot is literally "waters of rest."
webster_summary: Psalm 23:2 calm refreshing water; "waters of rest."
webster_full: Psalm 23:2's calm waters where the Shepherd leads the flock to drink. Sheep cannot drink from rushing or muddy streams; the Shepherd seeks out still pools or quiet eddies. The Hebrew mei menuchot is literally "waters of rest" — cognate of menuchah, the rest-word of Psalm 95:11. The same root underlies the name Noah.
scriptures: Psalm 23:2
He maketh me to lie down in green pastures: he leadeth me beside the still waters.
Isaiah 32:18
And my people shall dwell in a peaceable habitation, and in sure dwellings, and in quiet resting places.
Revelation 7:17
For the Lamb which is in the midst of the throne shall feed them, and shall lead them unto living fountains of waters.
corruption_summary: Romantic-poetry reading misses the practical sheep-physiology behind the image.
corruption_paragraphs: Sheep cannot drink from rushing streams; they panic and refuse. The Shepherd leads them specifically to still waters because that is the only kind they can use. The image is therefore more practical than poetic: the Shepherd's care knows what His sheep need.
Recover the practicality: the rest-waters are chosen by the Shepherd because the sheep require rest-waters. He knows.
usage: He leadeth me beside the still waters.
Sheep need still waters; the Shepherd knows.
Waters of rest, by careful choice.

etymology: Hebrew maglei tsedeq (Ps 23:3) — well-worn tracks of righteousness.
biblical_def: Psalm 23:3's image of the Shepherd leading along well-worn moral-spiritual tracks — not pioneering new ways, but following the righteousness-paths long established by the LORD. "For his name's sake" makes the leading more about His reputation than the saint's deserving.
webster_summary: Psalm 23:3 well-worn moral tracks the Shepherd uses.
webster_full: Psalm 23:3's image. The Hebrew maglei tsedeq are well-worn tracks (think trail-grooves) of righteousness. The Shepherd is not blazing trail; He is leading along paths long established by Himself across generations of saints. "For his name's sake" anchors the leading: His reputation, not our deserving, drives the route.
scriptures: Psalm 23:3
He restoreth my soul: he leadeth me in the paths of righteousness for his name's sake.
Proverbs 4:18
But the path of the just is as the shining light, that shineth more and more unto the perfect day.
Jeremiah 6:16
Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls.
corruption_summary: Modern preference for new and innovative paths misses Scripture's old-path commendation.
corruption_paragraphs: The age prizes innovation. Scripture commends the old paths (Jer 6:16) and the long-established tracks of righteousness. The Shepherd doesn't invent new routes; He leads along the ways saints have walked for millennia.
Recover the old paths: ask for them; walk therein; find rest for your souls. Innovation is not always better than the worn track.
usage: Paths of righteousness for His name's sake.
Ask for the old paths.
Innovation is not always better.

etymology: Hebrew kosi revayah (Ps 23:5) — literally "my cup is saturation."
biblical_def: Psalm 23:5's image of YHWH as host whose cup-pour for the saint exceeds the cup's capacity. The Hebrew revayah means saturation or abundance. The Shepherd is also Host; the table is in the presence of enemies; the cup overflows because the host's generosity exceeds the guest's capacity.
webster_summary: Psalm 23:5 host's pour exceeds the cup — abundance.
webster_full: Psalm 23:5's image of YHWH as host. The Shepherd-image of vv 1-4 shifts to a host-banquet image at v 5: "Thou preparest a table before me in the presence of mine enemies: thou anointest my head with oil; my cup runneth over." The Hebrew kosi revayah is "my cup [is] saturation" — abundance pouring past the brim. The host's generosity exceeds the guest's capacity to contain.
scriptures: Psalm 23:5
Thou preparest a table before me in the presence of mine enemies: thou anointest my head with oil; my cup runneth over.
Psalm 16:5
The LORD is the portion of mine inheritance and of my cup: thou maintainest my lot.
John 10:10
I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly.
corruption_summary: Prosperity teaching co-opts "cup runneth over" for material wealth; the Psalmic context is provision-in-the-midst-of-enemies.
corruption_paragraphs: Prosperity preachers love the cup-runneth-over image as material-wealth promise. The actual context: a table prepared in the presence of mine enemies. The cup overflows under threat, not in safety. The abundance is provision-while-besieged, not removal-of-besiegers.
Recover the context: the saint's cup overflows where enemies still surround. The host of Psalm 23:5 is the same Shepherd of Psalm 23:1, providing in danger as well as in calm.
usage: My cup runneth over — in the presence of enemies.
Provision-while-besieged, not removal-of-besiegers.
Host's generosity exceeds guest's capacity.

etymology: Hebrew beit YHWH; the dwelling of God's manifest presence among His people.
biblical_def: The dwelling of YHWH's manifest presence among His people. Tabernacle in the wilderness, temple in Jerusalem, eschatological New Jerusalem ("the tabernacle of God is with men," Rev 21:3). Psalm 23:6's "I will dwell in the house of the LORD for ever" anticipates the eschatological consummation; Psalm 27:4 names the saint's chief desire as dwelling there.
webster_summary: The dwelling of YHWH's manifest presence; tabernacle, temple, New Jerusalem.
webster_full: The dwelling of YHWH's manifest presence among His people across redemptive history: tabernacle in the wilderness, temple under Solomon, second temple post-exile, Christ Himself as the new temple (John 2:19-21), the church as living temple (1 Cor 3:16), and finally the eschatological consummation where "the tabernacle of God is with men" (Rev 21:3). Psalm 23:6's closing line and Psalm 27:4's chief desire both name dwelling there as the saint's deepest hope.
scriptures: Psalm 27:4
One thing have I desired of the LORD, that will I seek after; that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to behold the beauty of the LORD, and to enquire in his temple.
Psalm 84:10
For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand. I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness.
Psalm 23:6
Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life: and I will dwell in the house of the LORD for ever.
corruption_summary: Reduced to church-building references; misses the redemptive-historical sweep from tabernacle to New Jerusalem.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern "house of the LORD" often just means a church building. Scripture's beit YHWH sweeps from tabernacle through temple through Christ-the-temple through the church-as-temple to the New Jerusalem. The trajectory is real and deepening — not a building.
Recover the sweep: the saint already dwells in YHWH's house through Christ; will dwell there fully in the New Jerusalem; should orient life toward that final dwelling.
usage: Dwell in the house of the LORD for ever.
A day in His courts is better than a thousand.
Tabernacle to temple to Christ to New Jerusalem.

etymology: Hebrew simu levav-kem al darkei-kem (Hag 1:5, 7) — "set your heart upon your ways."
biblical_def: Haggai's twice-repeated post-exilic command to the returned community: take honest inventory of how your life is actually going. The command is diagnostic — sown much, harvested little; eaten, not satisfied; wages in a bag with holes — because the LORD's house lay neglected. Self-examination as honest accounting.
webster_summary: Take honest diagnostic inventory of your life's actual fruit.
webster_full: The Hebrew simu levav-kem al darkei-kem — "set your heart upon your ways" — is Haggai's diagnostic command twice in chapter 1 (vv 5, 7). The post-exilic returnees had built their own paneled houses while the LORD's house lay in ruins; the result was sown-much-harvested-little, eaten-not-satisfied, wages-in-a-bag-with-holes. Consider your ways: examine the actual fruit of your priorities.
scriptures: Haggai 1:5-6

Now therefore thus saith the LORD of hosts; Consider your ways. Ye have sown much, and bring in little; ye eat, but ye have not enough; ye drink, but ye are not filled with drink; ye clothe you, but there is none warm; and he that earneth wages earneth wages to put it into a bag with holes.
Haggai 1:7
Thus saith the LORD of hosts; Consider your ways.
Lamentations 3:40
Let us search and try our ways, and turn again to the LORD.
corruption_summary: Self-examination has been replaced by self-affirmation; "don't be too hard on yourself" has displaced "consider your ways."
corruption_paragraphs: Therapeutic culture trains us toward self-affirmation and away from self-examination. Haggai's command is diagnostic: look honestly at your life's fruit. Holes in the bag? Sown much for little? The diagnosis is the gift; the LORD calls because He is ready to fix it.
Recover the diagnostic: consider your ways. Honestly. The LORD doesn't condemn; He calls.
usage: Consider your ways — the diagnostic.
Sown much, harvested little? Bag with holes?
The diagnosis is the gift.

etymology: Hebrew al tira; recurring divine reassurance commanded ~365 times across Scripture (one for each day, by the lore-count).
biblical_def: The most-frequent divine command in Scripture: do not fear. Spoken to Abraham (Gen 15:1), Israel at the Red Sea (Exod 14:13), Joshua (Josh 1:9), Mary (Luke 1:30), the shepherds (Luke 2:10), and many more. Always grounded in God's presence: fear not, for I am with thee.
webster_summary: The most-frequent divine command; grounded always in His presence.
webster_full: Often cited as Scripture's most-frequent command — "do not fear" or "fear not" appears repeatedly across both testaments. Always grounded in God's presence: fear not, for I am with thee (Isa 41:10); fear not, for I have redeemed thee (Isa 43:1); fear not, for I am thy shield (Gen 15:1). The command is therapeutic only because the ground (God's presence) is real.
scriptures: Isaiah 41:10
Fear thou not; for I am with thee: be not dismayed; for I am thy God: I will strengthen thee; yea, I will help thee; yea, I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness.
Joshua 1:9
Have not I commanded thee? Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest.
Luke 2:10
And the angel said unto them, Fear not: for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people.
corruption_summary: Therapy-culture treats fear as something to manage technique-by-technique; Scripture answers it with God's presence.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern fear-management leans on techniques: breathing, mindfulness, exposure. Scripture's fear-not is grounded in a Person: the God who is with the saint. The technique is real but secondary; the presence is the substance.
Recover the ground: fear not, FOR. The conjunction is the work. He is with thee; therefore fear not. Without the ground, the command is empty.
usage: Fear not, FOR I am with thee.
The conjunction does the work.
Most-frequent divine command.

etymology: Hebrew chazaq; Joshua 1's repeated divine charge.
biblical_def: The divine command to take courageous strength, given as preparation for the conquest in Joshua 1 ("be strong and of a good courage" appears three times in 1:6, 7, 9). Strength in Scripture is rarely raw; it is courage rooted in God's presence and command. "Quit you like men, be strong" (1 Cor 16:13) renews the charge for the church.
webster_summary: Divine charge to courageous strength rooted in His presence.
webster_full: The Hebrew chazaq — be strong — appears three times in Joshua 1 (vv 6, 7, 9) as YHWH's preparing charge for the conquest. Strength in Scripture is courage with content: rooted in God's presence ("the LORD thy God is with thee"), grounded in His word ("do not turn from it to the right hand or to the left"), oriented toward action ("go in unto Canaan"). Paul renews the charge in 1 Cor 16:13 ("be strong").
scriptures: Joshua 1:9
Have not I commanded thee? Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest.
Deuteronomy 31:6
Be strong and of a good courage, fear not, nor be afraid of them: for the LORD thy God, he it is that doth go with thee; he will not fail thee, nor forsake thee.
1 Corinthians 16:13
Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong.
corruption_summary: Modern "be strong" is often raw self-reliance; biblical strength is courage rooted in God's presence and command.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern strength-talk is often individualistic and raw: tough it out, push through, you've got this. Biblical strength is different: rooted in His presence, oriented by His word, directed toward His call. "Be strong and of a good courage" is followed immediately by "for the LORD thy God is with thee."
Recover the for-clause: strength has a source. Without it, the command is hollow.
usage: Be strong and of a good courage.
Strength has a source: His presence.
Quit you like men; be strong.

etymology: Hebrew zeroot olam (Deut 33:27) — arms of eternity. Moses' final blessing of Israel.
biblical_def: Moses' final-blessing image of YHWH's eternal sustaining strength: "The eternal God is thy refuge, and underneath are the everlasting arms" (Deut 33:27). The arms hold from below — you cannot fall lower than they reach. The basis of the great hymn "Leaning on the Everlasting Arms."
webster_summary: Moses' final-blessing image: God's arms hold from below.
webster_full: Image from Moses' final blessing of Israel before his death (Deut 33:27): "The eternal God is thy refuge, and underneath are the everlasting arms." The Hebrew zeroot olam — arms of eternity — describes God's eternal sustaining strength positioned below the saint, so falling cannot exceed His reach. Anthony Showalter's 1887 hymn "Leaning on the Everlasting Arms" carries the imagery into Christian devotion.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 33:27
The eternal God is thy refuge, and underneath are the everlasting arms: and he shall thrust out the enemy from before thee; and shall say, Destroy them.
Isaiah 40:11
He shall feed his flock like a shepherd: he shall gather the lambs with his arm, and carry them in his bosom.
Isaiah 46:4
And even to your old age I am he; and even to hoar hairs will I carry you: I have made, I will bear, even I will carry, and will deliver you.
corruption_summary: Sentimentalized as soft comfort; the actual image is muscular sustaining-strength positioned below.
corruption_paragraphs: "Leaning on the Everlasting Arms" sounds gentle. The Mosaic image is muscular: arms positioned below, ready to catch any fall. The eternal God is below you, holding. You cannot fall lower than He reaches.
Recover the position: His arms are below, not just above. The fall has a floor; the floor is His strength.
usage: Underneath are the everlasting arms.
His arms are below; the fall has a floor.
Eternal God; eternal sustaining.

etymology: Hebrew rum with the divine object — to lift up, magnify, raise high.
biblical_def: The verb of declaring YHWH's greatness publicly. Psalm 34:3's communal call: "O magnify the LORD with me, and let us exalt his name together." Exaltation is not adding to God's greatness (impossible) but declaring it openly — to ourselves, to one another, before the nations.
webster_summary: To declare YHWH's greatness publicly.
webster_full: The verb of declaring YHWH's greatness aloud, especially in worship and witness. Hebrew rum means to lift up, raise high. We do not add to God's height; we declare it. Psalm 34:3 makes it communal: "let us exalt his name together." Exaltation as worship is verbal raising-aloud of what is already true.
scriptures: Psalm 34:3
O magnify the LORD with me, and let us exalt his name together.
Psalm 99:5
Exalt ye the LORD our God, and worship at his footstool; for he is holy.
Isaiah 25:1
O LORD, thou art my God; I will exalt thee, I will praise thy name; for thou hast done wonderful things.
corruption_summary: Worship-language has thinned; "exalt" gets reduced to "praise generally" without the lift-up-aloud force.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern worship-vocabulary leans on "praise." Hebrew has more colors: rum (exalt, lift high), halal (praise, shine), yadah (give thanks publicly), barak (bless on bended knee). Each carries a different shade.
Recover the colors: exalt is the lift-aloud verb. Take what is true of God and lift it where others can hear.
roots_lines: to be high, lift up, exalt
usage: Let us exalt his name together.
Verbal lifting-aloud of what is true.
Communal exaltation before the nations.

etymology: Hebrew shuv with YHWH; the prophetic call to repentance.
biblical_def: The prophetic call par excellence: turn back to YHWH from idols, sin, exile, indifference. Hebrew shuv is the verb of repentance, used hundreds of times. "Return unto me, and I will return unto you, saith the LORD of hosts" (Mal 3:7). The two-way verb of covenant restoration.
webster_summary: The prophetic call to turn back to YHWH; the verb of repentance.
webster_full: Hebrew shuv, the verb of return / repentance, used hundreds of times in the OT. The prophetic call to Israel across centuries: return to YHWH. The two-way structure of Mal 3:7 ("Return unto me, and I will return unto you") and Zech 1:3 names the covenant restoration: human turning meets divine turning. Repentance in Scripture is fundamentally directional — from idols and sin toward YHWH.
scriptures: Hosea 6:1
Come, and let us return unto the LORD: for he hath torn, and he will heal us; he hath smitten, and he will bind us up.
Malachi 3:7
Even from the days of your fathers ye are gone away from mine ordinances, and have not kept them. Return unto me, and I will return unto you, saith the LORD of hosts.
Therefore also now, saith the LORD, turn ye even to me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning.
corruption_summary: Modern repentance-language often centers on feelings ("feel sorry") rather than on the directional verb (turn back).
corruption_paragraphs: Pop repentance is feelings-heavy: be sorry, feel bad, do better. Hebrew shuv is directional: turn back. The feelings may follow; the verb leads. You can shuv without intense emotion if the direction-change is real.
Recover the verb: return. Turn around. The LORD answers with His own returning — "and I will return unto you." Two-way verb.
usage: Return unto me, and I will return unto you.
Repentance is directional: turn back.
Two-way verb: human and divine returning meet.

etymology: Hebrew ranan, rua; the loud joyful cry commanded throughout Psalms.
biblical_def: The audible loud joyful cry commanded as worship-response throughout Psalms. Not silent inner happiness but outward voiced jubilation. "Make a joyful noise unto the LORD, all the earth" (Ps 100:1). Worship in Scripture has volume.
webster_summary: Audible loud joyful cry; worship has volume.
webster_full: The Hebrew rua means a loud cry, a shout, a war-cry; ranan emphasizes joyful jubilation. Both appear repeatedly in Psalms as worship-imperatives. "Make a joyful noise unto the LORD" (Ps 95:1; 100:1) is a shout-command. Israel shouted at Jericho; the temple-builders shouted when the foundation was laid; saints shout for joy when YHWH delivers.
scriptures: Psalm 100:1
Make a joyful noise unto the LORD, all ye lands.
Psalm 5:11
But let all those that put their trust in thee rejoice: let them ever shout for joy, because thou defendest them: let them also that love thy name be joyful in thee.
And all the people shouted with a great shout, when they praised the LORD, because the foundation of the house of the LORD was laid.
corruption_summary: Reverence-only worship culture has muted the shout; biblical worship makes noise.
corruption_paragraphs: Some Christian traditions equate reverence with silence. Scripture knows reverent silence (Hab 2:20) and reverent shouting (Ps 100:1) — both are worship. Israel shouted at Jericho's walls; saints shout when foundations are laid. Worship has volume.
Recover the shout: make a joyful noise. Volume is not the enemy of reverence; both are commanded.
usage: Make a joyful noise unto the LORD.
Worship in Scripture has volume.
Reverent silence and reverent shouting both commanded.

etymology: Hebrew nir nir lakem (Hos 10:12; Jer 4:3) — break up the unplowed land of your hearts.
biblical_def: The agricultural metaphor for repentance — breaking up the hardened, untilled ground of the heart so that the seed of God's word can take root. Hosea 10:12 issues the call: "Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap in mercy; break up your fallow ground: for it is time to seek the LORD." Jeremiah 4:3 repeats it. Spiritual revival begins with broken plowed-up ground.
webster_summary: Repentance-as-agriculture: break up the hardened heart-ground.
webster_full: Agricultural metaphor for the deep work of repentance. Hebrew nir is fallow ground — uncultivated, hardened, weed-grown. The plow must break it up before seed can take. Hosea 10:12 issues the imperative; Jeremiah 4:3 repeats it. Spiritual revival in Scripture begins with this kind of plowing — the deep, uncomfortable, soul-tearing breaking-up of long-hardened ground.
scriptures: Hosea 10:12
Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap in mercy; break up your fallow ground: for it is time to seek the LORD, till he come and rain righteousness upon you.
Jeremiah 4:3
Thus saith the LORD to the men of Judah and Jerusalem, Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns.
Psalm 51:17
The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise.
corruption_summary: Comfortable Christianity skips the plowing; revival requires it.
corruption_paragraphs: Easy Christianity wants harvest without plowing. The prophets insist: there is no harvest in fallow ground. The plow is uncomfortable, expensive, slow. But until the hardened ground breaks up, the seed cannot take root.
Recover the plowing: break up the heart's fallow ground. Long-neglected sins, long-hardened patterns, long-comfortable compromises — plow them up before the next planting.
usage: Break up your fallow ground.
No harvest in fallow ground.
Plow before planting; revive before reviving.

etymology: Hebrew yarash erets; recurring covenant promise of land-inheritance.
biblical_def: The covenant promise of land-inheritance: to Abraham (Gen 12-15), to Israel under Moses and Joshua, and eschatologically to the meek ("the meek shall inherit the earth," Ps 37:11; quoted Matt 5:5). Concrete and physical — not just spiritual abstract; the renewed earth is the saint's eternal portion.
webster_summary: Covenant promise of land; physical, not just spiritual.
webster_full: The covenant promise of land-inheritance running from Abraham (Gen 12-15) through the Mosaic conquest and allotment under Joshua, into the eschatological promise that "the meek shall inherit the earth" (Ps 37:11; Matt 5:5). The promise is concrete: actual land, real soil, eternal possession. The renewed earth of Revelation 21 is the consummation of this trajectory.
scriptures: Psalm 37:11
But the meek shall inherit the earth; and shall delight themselves in the abundance of peace.
Matthew 5:5
Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth.
Romans 4:13
For the promise, that he should be the heir of the world, was not to Abraham, or to his seed, through the law, but through the righteousness of faith.
corruption_summary: Spiritualized away from the concrete renewed earth; the meek often pictured as inheriting heaven, not earth.
corruption_paragraphs: Christ said the meek inherit the earth, not the clouds. The biblical eschaton is renewed creation, not disembodied spirit-existence. Romans 4:13 makes Abraham heir of the world. Land theology runs from Genesis to Revelation.
Recover the concreteness: the saint's inheritance is the renewed earth, ruled by Christ, where righteousness dwells (2 Pet 3:13). Concrete soil, eternal Sabbath.
usage: The meek shall inherit the earth.
Land theology is concrete.
Abraham heir of the world; saints heirs through faith.

etymology: Hebrew maqor mayim chayyim; YHWH as the source-spring of life-giving water.
biblical_def: YHWH's self-description in Jeremiah 2:13 as "the fountain of living waters" against which Israel had committed two evils — forsaken Him and hewn out broken cisterns. Christ takes up the imagery in John 4:10-14 with the Samaritan woman and John 7:37-38 with the rivers-of-living-water from the believer's belly.
webster_summary: YHWH (and Christ) as the source-spring of life-giving water.
webster_full: Hebrew maqor mayim chayyim — "fountain of living waters." YHWH's self-description in Jeremiah 2:13: "my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water." Christ takes up the image in John 4 (the well of water springing up to everlasting life within the believer) and John 7 (rivers of living water flowing out from the believer's belly — identified as the Spirit).
scriptures: Jeremiah 2:13
For my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water.

Whosoever drinketh of this water shall thirst again: But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life.
If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink. He that believeth on me, as the saith hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water.
corruption_summary: Both Jewish and Christian readers can drift into broken-cistern self-help; only the source-spring water never runs out.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeremiah names two evils: forsaking the spring AND hewing broken cisterns. Self-help spirituality, self-improvement religion, self-curated identity — all are broken cisterns. They look like they hold water; they leak.
Recover the source: living water comes only from the source-spring. Drink there; the well becomes within you; rivers flow from you.
usage: Forsook the spring; hewed broken cisterns.
Drink of the spring; well becomes within.
Rivers of living water from the believer's belly.

etymology: Hebrew shachah; the bodily prostration that constitutes biblical worship.
biblical_def: The Hebrew word usually translated "worship" is shachah — literally to bow down, prostrate oneself. Biblical worship is bodily before it is musical or verbal: knees bent, face down, body lower than head. The first commandment forbids bowing to other gods (Exod 20:5) precisely because bowing is what worship physically is.
webster_summary: The bodily prostration that biblically constitutes worship.
webster_full: Hebrew shachah, the most-frequent OT verb translated "worship," literally means to bow down, prostrate oneself. Biblical worship is bodily before it is musical or verbal: knees bent, face to ground, body lower than mind. The first commandment forbids bowing to other gods (Exod 20:5) because bowing IS worship. The Magi fell down and worshipped (Matt 2:11).
scriptures: Psalm 95:6
O come, let us worship and bow down: let us kneel before the LORD our maker.
Matthew 2:11
And when they were come into the house, they saw the young child with Mary his mother, and fell down, and worshipped him.
Revelation 4:10
The four and twenty elders fall down before him that sat on the throne, and worship him that liveth for ever and ever.
corruption_summary: Modern "worship" is often almost entirely musical; the bodily prostration that the Hebrew verb names is largely lost.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern worship-services rarely involve actual bowing. Hebrew shachah is bowing; Greek proskuneō (the NT equivalent) means to fall toward and kiss the ground. The body is part of worship in Scripture — not optional.
Recover the body: kneel, prostrate, bow. The body teaches the soul. The Magi fell down; the elders fall down; the saint should fall down too.
usage: Worship is bodily — bowing is the verb.
Kneel before the LORD our maker.
The Magi fell down; the elders fall down.

etymology: Hebrew tsaphan (to hide, treasure up) + leb (heart); Psalm 119:11.
biblical_def: Psalm 119:11's discipline of treasuring God's word internally as defense against sin: "Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee." Memorization and meditation as protective storage of Scripture in the inner core of the person.
webster_summary: Psalm 119:11 discipline of internal Scripture-treasuring.
webster_full: Psalm 119:11's discipline: tsaphan means to hide, store up, treasure. The psalmist treasures Scripture internally as protection against sin. Memorization and deep meditation are the practical means; the heart (leb, the integrated inner core) is the storehouse. The hidden word becomes available in the moment of temptation when the open Bible is not.
scriptures: Psalm 119:11
Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee.
Deuteronomy 6:6
And these words, which I command thee this day, shall be in thine heart.
Colossians 3:16
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.
corruption_summary: Memorization is largely abandoned in modern Christianity; the hidden-word availability has thinned with it.
corruption_paragraphs: Smartphones make Scripture accessible everywhere; this has discouraged memorization. But in the moment of temptation, the heart that has hidden the word has the word. The phone may not be charged; the heart is.
Recover the discipline: hide His word. Memorize. Meditate. The hidden word is what stands at 3 AM.
usage: Thy word have I hid in mine heart.
Memorize what may not be at hand.
Hidden word stands at 3 AM.

etymology: Old English heorcnian; KJV's standard rendering of Hebrew shama (to hear, listen, obey).
biblical_def: KJV's standard rendering of shama — to hear-and-obey. The Hebrew verb does not split listening from obeying; biblical hearing already implies the obedient response. The Shema ("Hear, O Israel") opens with this verb. To hearken is the saint's first and continuing posture before the LORD's word.
webster_summary: KJV verb for hearing-and-obeying; biblical hearing implies response.
webster_full: Older English verb meaning to hear with attention, often with the implication of heeding or obeying. KJV's standard rendering of Hebrew shama (the verb of the Shema). The Hebrew refuses to split listening from obeying: to hear truly is to obey. The disobedient ear has not really heard. Hearkening is therefore not just attention but the active surrender of will.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 6:4
Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD.
Isaiah 55:2-3
Hearken diligently unto me, and eat ye that which is good, and let your soul delight itself in fatness. Incline your ear, and come unto me: hear, and your soul shall live.
1 Samuel 15:22
Hath the LORD as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the LORD? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice.
corruption_summary: Modern English splits hearing (passive) from obeying (active); Hebrew refuses the split.
corruption_paragraphs: We speak of hearing without obeying as if they are independent. Hebrew shama refuses: to hear and not obey is not really to have heard. Modern translations sometimes lose the force; KJV's "hearken" preserves it.
Recover the unity: hearken means hear-and-obey. Half is not hearkening.
usage: Hearken diligently unto me.
Hearing without obeying is not hearkening.
To obey is better than sacrifice.
